newsitem.title: New Zealand: NZ debt faces US data hurdle after depressing week.
newsitem.headline: NZ debt faces US data hurdle after depressing week.

text.p: Figures in brackets compare against previous day's close
FUTURES PHYSICAL YIELD (PCT)
90-DAY BILLS (JUN) 91.90 (PREV 91.93) 90-DAYS 7.97 (PREV 7.93)
OVERNIGHT CASH 7.50 PCT (PREV 7.45) US 5-YR 6.71 (PREV 6.72)
* NZ yields end higher, but down from opening levels
* Money market also suffers from bearish sentiment
U.S. jobs data awaited but may not be the fillip needed
New Zealand debt markets ended the week on a very soft note on Friday after sharply underperforming U.S. and Australian debt on the spreads
Bond yields came back slightly from their early selling, but the mid bond yields still ended seven basis points higher at 8.16 percent, while the 11/06 was off three at 8.18 percent.
Dealers said the early selling had been slightly overdone and that had been corrected, but it was difficult to read too much into the small improvement during the session.
"People weren't necessarily thinking it was time to buy at 8.25 percent (in the 11/06s) -- there was no great flurry of activity with people saying this is too cheap," one dealer said.
"Really there's nothing to say, we shouldn't be at 8.50 percent as much as going back to 8.00."
In the money market, key 90-day bank bills managed to finish below 8.00 percent after an early break of the figure, and closed four basis points softer at 7.97 percent.
The June futures contract was also off four at 91.90, on light volume of 445 contracts.
Cash bumped back up to 7.50 percent after a short-lived flirtation with 7.45 percent.

U.S. March non-farm payrolls data due at 1330 GMT is expected to help set the scene for next week's trade, but dealers warned a good number may not be sufficient to prod New Zealand bonds out of their misery.
Economists polled by Reuters expect on average an increase of 196,000 in non-farm payrolls and a rise in average hourly wages of 0.4 percent.
One local dealer said the jobs data was the first hurdle for New Zealand bonds to overcome.
"The second is to try to identify whether there are more sellers of New Zealand bonds out there as there have been for two days. If that's true, we will go higher.

"If it's a good number and the U.S. rallies we might get back a few points, but we won't get back to 8.00 percent (in the 10-year bond) because we've gone up 20 points on the fact that someone was selling local bonds," he said.
